report:
## Conclusion

Your claim is well supported: among adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), bystander hands-only (chest-compression–only) CPR is associated with higher survival than receiving no bystander CPR.

The most directly relevant evidence is a prospective Arizona cohort study (2005–09) of 4,415 adult OHCAs, which compared no bystander CPR, conventional CPR, and layperson compression-only CPR. After adjustment for relevant differences, compression-only CPR was associated with greater survival to hospital discharge than *both* no bystander CPR and conventional CPR. This is strong real-world association evidence, but it remains observational—people who receive CPR may differ in ways that also affect prognosis (for example, arrest being witnessed or occurring in public).  
https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/186668

Evidence also supports hands-only CPR as a practical alternative to conventional CPR for adult presumed cardiac arrests. A randomized dispatcher-instruction trial compared compression-only with standard CPR and assessed 30-day survival; this helps establish that omitting breaths does not negate the benefit of prompt compressions in the typical adult cardiac-arrest scenario.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0908991

The American Heart Association’s scientific advisory concluded that hands-only CPR can reduce delay and interruptions and that adults receiving hands-only or conventional bystander CPR have similar survival chances.  
https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/circulationaha.107.189380

**Important qualification:** This does not mean breaths are never important. Hands-only CPR is principally for adults with sudden collapse of likely cardiac origin; conventional CPR with breaths is especially important in drowning, overdose/respiratory arrest, and pediatric arrests. But versus doing nothing, immediate hands-only CPR is the evidence-based action for an unresponsive adult who is not breathing normally.
